Management: Good evening, everyone, and a very warm welcome to PB Fintech Limited Earnings Conference Call
Q2FY27. Thank you for joining us today. On the call today, we have:
• Mr. Yashish Dahiya, Chairman & Group CEO, PB Fintech
• Mr. Alok Bansal, Executive Vice Chairman, PB Fintech
• Mr. Sarbvir Singh, Joint Group CEO, PB Fintech
• Ms. Santosh Agarwal, CEO, Paisabazaar
• Mr. Dhruv Sarin, CEO, PB Partners
• Mr. Mandeep Mehta, Group CFO, PB Fintech, and
• Mr. Mohit Khobragade, Head, Investor Relations, PB Fintech
We will begin with opening remarks from the management, followed by Q&A session. I now invite Yashish to share
his opening remarks. Over to you, Yashish.
Management: Thank you, Mohit. Good afternoon, good evening, good morning to everyone, wherever you are joining
from. Thank you for joining us. We've had another strong quarter with healthy growth across insurance and credit.
The total insurance premium for the quarter was ₹9,385 Cr, up 38% year-on-year, setting us up well for over ₹40,000
Cr this year. As always, growth was led by protection, because that's our focus from day one, and continues to be our
focus. Core online new health and term grew 42% YoY, and within this, new health grew 46% YoY. Consolidated
operating revenue grew 35% to ₹2,178 Cr. Core insurance revenue was up 42% YoY and core credit revenue, up 19%
YoY. PAT grew 43% to ₹192 Cr, and PAT margin improved from 8% to 9%. The quality of this growth shows in its
consistency. Core new premium, excluding savings, has now grown at above 34% for 14 consecutive quarters. And
our core renewal and trail revenue is now over ₹1,000 Cr, it's almost ₹1,100 Cr. On a rolling 12-month basis, up 42%
year-on-year. In credit, disbursals grew 22% in the core business and this has now risen for 5 consecutive quarters.
Our insurance-led new initiatives, PB Partners, UAE Business, and PB for Business, delivered ₹826 Cr of revenue, up
40% and are now close to break-even. UAE Premium grew 36% YoY.
Let me now address the question straight up, which I'm assuming is on everybody's mind. First of all, where do we
stand on IRDAI's consultation paper? IRDAI's consultation paper aims for lower mis-selling, better claims experience,
lower prices, and deeper penetration. We absolutely support all of these goals fully. These are the goals Policybazaar
was built on. Our first campaign back in 2009 was ‘Ullu Mat Bano’, aimed at addressing mis-selling. We have engaged
constructively with the regulator, and we will implement the final framework fully, and in its spirit. Second, the impact.
Lower distribution payouts will reduce our insurance distribution revenue, for sure. We are working on three fronts.
We will expand our non-insurance revenue within and as the regulator permits and there is some anticipation that
could happen. In the discussion paper, it does mention that. We will accelerate our ecosystem offerings. And as any
long-term business should, we are evaluating other options to strengthen our business over time. We will share much
more on this as and when the time is appropriate. Now, why do we remain confident? Health and term insurance stay
deeply under-penetrated. And for the consumer, it's not really about buying the policy. The customer gets nothing on
the day he buys it. The real test comes at claims. And I would like to just cover our record. On the four points that the
regulators themselves lay out. On claims in the health insurance industry, the industry data says 87% of health claims
are settled. That same number for Policybazaar customers is 97%. Last year, 11,156 rejected claims worth ₹185 Cr
were reopened after initial rejection and paid. In the first half of this year alone, we supported about 1.25 lakh health
claims and 80,000 motor claims. Our customer satisfaction is consistently above 90%. On persistency, 71% of our life
policies are still in force at month 61. This is against a benchmark of 51% to 66% for the large players. Our renewal in
health insurance is at 89%, rising to 91% from second-year renewals onwards. On mis-selling, in the life insurance
category, we get 16 complaints from our customers per 10,000 customers. This is against a benchmark of 30 to 53. In
health insurance, we get 21 claim complaints for every 10,000 claims. This is against a benchmark of 29 to 54. On

Page 2 of 14
price reduction, for the plans they choose, our health customers pay, on average, 9% less and up to 30% less than
some other channels. And on reach and expansion of the market, about 40% of new customers added in Retail Health
across the country come through us. More than a quarter of India's pure term premium, 17.8% of the retail health
premium came through us last year. 74% of our term policies and 64% of our health policies come from Tier 2 and
Tier 3 cities. These outcomes are very much required in the country and that is why we, as a management team, are
super confident that we solve this particular problem. We are a part of the solution, and we will only grow stronger
through this. Our credit business and our UAE business are growing, and outside this broad framework. We will
maintain strict cost discipline over the years as we go through this period. What will we not do? While maintaining
this cost discipline, and profitability focus, we will not cut back on the customer proposition. Not one step back on
that. Choice, transparency, and claim support remain non-negotiable. We will remain fully compliant and consult with
the regulator on whatever we do in this area. Finally, since our listing, quarterly revenue has grown from ₹280 Cr to
₹2,178 Cr, a 51% CAGR, and the PAT margin has moved from -73% to 9%. That came from building around what
customers need. And we have a very clear, let's call it, mission, or strategy, whatever you want to call it. Over the next
1000 days, we will serve customers well, we will stay focused on that, we will stay disciplined on cost, and we will
keep investing in a market that remains deeply underpenetrated. It's a very simple strategy. Thank you. Look forward
to your questions.
Management: Thank you, Yashish. We will now move to the Q&A session.
Management: We will take the first question from the line of Sachin Salgaonkar from BofA. Sachin, please unmute
your mic.
Sachin Salgaonkar: Hi Mohit, thank you. Good day, management. I have 3 questions. First question, want to
understand anything specific happened in the quarter which led to an increase in selling and marketing expenses and
other expenses, both in terms of QoQ as well as YoY.
Management: Sachin, two things have happened. Last year, because of the GST impact and everything, and I think it
was kind of pre-GST, although this quarter. But somehow, last year, from June to, obviously till December, the demand
was very robust, and which meant that we spent, I would say, lower than our normal level of spending in marketing.
This year, it's been the reverse. Actually, demand has been very tough, and I think we've had to spend a lot more
money. So I would say that if you look at it on a two-year basis, you'll find it's not that dramatic. But yeah, versus last
year, it will look as if it was higher. And it was just lack of demand in the market, and I think we had to spend money
to make sure that we got the leads.
Sachin Salgaonkar: Got it. And, to follow up on this, how should we think about the incremental spending in next,
let's say, 3 to 6 months? And I'm asking from a point of view that there is this entire overhang associated in terms of
these commission structure gets implemented. Is there a school of thought that it would make sense to control costs,
particularly the discretionary items, and show contribution margin improvement. In the opening remark, Yashish did
mention about being disciplined from a cost point of view. And how do you look to sort of, balance it in context of
what you indicated, that from a demand point of view, things are a bit tough in the near term?
Management: Thanks, Sachin. Look, philosophically, earlier, we were only focused on growth. And, when we say that,
P0, P1, P2, P3, everything was growth. And we could have been a little aggressive on cost, because that was not the
highest priority. Now, that does not imply we were wasteful. As we move forward, the cost consciousness will be
there, but that does not mean we are backing off from growth. I think growth stays very critical in this market. Two
things. First of all, the market needs it. And I think in a way, scale is very important. And thus, we are going to keep

the focus on growth. However, yes, we will be more conscious about the balance between growth and cost than we
were in the past.
Management: I think Yashish said it right, Sachin. I think we will be more conscious of the balance, but having said

The only thing that you can't manage is demand. So, I think, we will have to spend money to keep the awareness to
continue with the focus on building the categories. And, frankly speaking, I think it doesn't impact just Policybazaar, I
think it impacts the industry, because, when we advertise, it helps everyone, and I think that's something that we will
have to keep doing.

Management: I don't think we are actively considering anything in the international space, as of now. And I think, on
Paisabazaar, we are doing everything we can, so it is not like our stance changes in any way. PB Health was and is a
very important project, which, we are doing, so that continues. I think, as we said. There are many ecosystem activities
that we do. We may have had a certain time frame on those. That timeframe starts to speed up a little bit. Also from
a revenue expectation, that increases from those areas. So, I guess that is how it would be. And we have been in
discussions with the regulator on various other options for us. And as and when we have clarity, we will, of course
announce them. There is no point announcing them in advance of regulatory approval. So, we will take that approval,
and once we have that, we will definitely inform the market.
Sachin Salgaonkar: This is very helpful, thanks a lot.
Management: Thank you, Sachin. We will now take the next question from the line of Manas Agarwal from Bernstein.

Management: See, you know it as well as I know it, Nidhesh. Let's look at the POSP business. We do make a loss there
today. I think the way the regulations are, that entire business is a bit under a question mark because to an extent, it

And how we were looking to expand our proposition. I don't think you're gonna see anything which is dramatically

Then, of course, our variable costs will also be markedly different. And, I think even on the fixed cost side. See, please
appreciate, as we said, we are going to be accelerating our ecosystem, we are looking at new offerings, a lot of our
current management, we are very unlikely to hire external people to be running those. So, a lot of the current
management will get repurposed. And I think, from a current management perspective, that is a fairly exciting

Management: I just want to add to what Yashish is saying. See, one of the things that we have to understand is that
in 2026, in a way, one very big force in the whole world today is AI, or GenAI. Now, if you think about it, for the last
18 months, we have been preparing. Because it takes time, see, whatever we all read about in the papers and, on
websites, etc., but the fact is, for a running organization, it takes time for these technologies to bite, and for them to
start becoming real. And if you ask me personally, I believe that in the last 18 months, we have done a lot of work.
There are some slides in the deck about the improvement that we have made, whether in terms of our advisor's ability
to handle 15-20% more leads, improve conversion. On the customer service side, on the risk side, on our ability to
train our people faster than we used to earlier. So, my view is that there's a bunch of factors that will be at play in the
next 12 to 18 months, and I think we will drive these technological changes also faster. See, finally, necessity is the
mother of invention. Now, today we understand that we cannot afford a certain cost to serve or to do certain things.
So, we will have to work out other ways, and I think this Gen AI has come at exactly the right time for us in that
respect. And, again, our teams are very excited about this. We are using it as you would expect, and I think that this
will also help us, in the next few years, going forward. So yeah, I mean, it's hard to quantify, it's hard to give you really
big numbers today, but my view is that, as a lever, since you asked for what levers do we have, I think AI is a very big
lever for Policybazaar to become a lot more efficient.
Nidhesh Jain: Sure. And secondly, do you see a scenario where you will return back to cash burn scenario, or will still

Management: I think, Nidhesh, to be brutally honest, we need to wait a little bit for the final regulations to come out.
See, the way the regulator has placed the discussion paper, the regulators themselves have said this is a discussion
paper. And they have undergone intense discussions since bringing out the regulation papers. And they're receiving

feedbacks from many quarters, more than 1,000 feedbacks have already reached the regulator. And I think, let them

thinking about the situation because, if anything, the cash position is a position of capability. Because if the NPV is
there and the cash is not there, that can assist us in that time frame. Mentally, the intent is not a cash burn intent.

Obviously being an insurance-heavy entity.
Management: See, I think Paisabazaar is that entity. Policybazaar will continue to be centered on insurance. Its

let's look at the regulations in the final form as they come out. See, when the final regulations, we have to see, how

be allowed again. And it could possibly open up and it's an advantage that we have Paisabazaar already ready with
lots of products, not just credit, but also the investment products. And we see that as a massive opportunity. But let

but it would be Paisabazaar offerings being utilized in Policybazaar to some extent, but not becoming the primary, as

Page 6 of 14
Nischint Chawathe: Got it. And, are you open to, sort of, extend software services support to insurance companies
which is not distribution of their products, but for some of the other channels.
Management: So, we already do that, and in fact it's a bit unknown, but the Bahrain government's financial platform
is being powered by us. So, there is clearly both an ability and an intention to power more and more people's
technology and operational backends. There is no doubt about it. And, yeah, we will, of course, keep exploring that.
So, it's not a new thing, that we already have.
Nischint Chawathe: And just finally, PB Health, how does this feature into it? Any thoughts on that?
Management: Look, let's be crystal clear here. Today, what problems do we have as an industry. Let us say claims is
a massive problem. I don't think anybody's denying that health insurance claims is a massive problem. Why is that
problem there? If you actually look at why claims are denied, a large component of it is either some level of pre-
existing diseases which existed but were not disclosed, so, disclosure problems. And the second large part of it is, at
some level, treatment not required, et cetera, et cetera. I believe we can't run that way. See, the health insurance
achieved a lot. And I'll want to explain this in just some brief data points. Back in 2008, 1% of hospitals' bills used to
be settled by retail health insurance and insurance per se. Then it became about 10%, and today about 40% of
hospitals' bills are being settled by insurance. So, there is massive growth in healthcare costs being addressed by
insurance. Massive growth. But still, we have a lot of negativity around claims. And that negativity is coming from
these two problems. Disclosure, and the ability to align the network. The job Policybazaar historically did was of better
disclosures. And increasingly, has been doing of better network management. And in that network management,
creating a benchmark for let us say consumer lifetime value, will be PB Health. Not from the highest profit perspective,
but from how the customer ought to be treated without an intent to make the maximum from the customer on every
visit. This is something PB Health has to do, and we started this project, and there's no change in our thought process
on that. It is neither speeding up, not slowing down. But yeah, some of the associated activities like PB Care+, etc,
which were around network management. Those, of course, are ever more important, as if claims is a problem, then
claims need to be solved, and, we have to be part of the solution.
Nischint Chawathe: No change in the business plan, I think that's what I was looking at.
Management: No, no change in that particular business plan.
Nischint Chawathe: Got it. Thank you very much.
Management: Thank you Nischint. Our next question is from the line of Jayant Kharote, from Axis. Jayant, please
unmute yourself.
Jayant Kharote: Hi, first question is on the POSP business. Last time, we did not have a clear answer because the
regulations were fresh. Have you had a chance to talk to your POSP partners, given the value we bring to the table.

Management: Jayanth, look, if you really look at the POSP business, a lot of it was motor insurance. And it is not
because that POSP was there, that that business was happening, to a large extent. Yes, some of the health insurance
business and some of the other business, there would have been some growth because of the POSP business. The
way the current regulations are, it says, if you are open architecture, you're going to get paid less than the closed
architecture. That in my opinion, does not leave scope for POSP the way it is today. Now, if POSP becomes a totally

different business, like maybe a services player or something of that sort, then maybe there is some possibility. I don't

watch. And, we stay observant. And, like, we're waiting. We're waiting for the final regulations, and I hope, time is

POSPs sooner than we get paid by the insurance companies. So, there are also those concerns. So, let's see how that
happens, right? It's about many, many parts, and given that, I hope, some time is given to transition on that business.

Management: So, I will let Alok answer on the plans and on how we are against our target for March, from a revenue
standpoint. In terms of stake, no, we want to maintain our stake at present. We are not expanding it, nor reducing it.
Management: In terms of the execution on PB Health's side, things haven't changed actually, in the last one quarter.
We are on track of executing a few new hospitals. So, around March, we should have a run rate somewhere between
₹40-45 Cr per month, which is about ₹500 Cr for the year. That’s because some of these are running hospitals. You

Management: Yeah, nothing is specific right now. I think, let's understand the lay of the land. I think, as I said, once
we have 3 to 5 properties which we are managing. It will be a steep learning curve for everyone in the team. And, at
some point in about, you can say, 18 months onwards. We start to look at those sort of options, but still a bit far away.
Jayant Kharote: Understood. And last question, to Yashish again. So, see, we will probably become a very highly
profitable business with the new commission structure, right? The COR moves to maybe 65% in, let's say, health, for
example. How do you capture that economic value? So, why not take up minority stakes in an insurer? Have you
thought about something like that? I mean, I understand there could be plans to go back and become manufacturing
yourself, but instead, what if it can be done through minority stakes in manufacturers rather than the entire value
chain?
Management: Jayant, we think of a lot of options. Taking minority stakes is not one of them. And all I can say is, we
are already in conversations with the regulator, of course, in formal conversations. And, there is clear precedent and
laws out there, and of course, we will engage with the regulator further and seek their guidance on how they want to
see this. But yes, the intent is quite clear in our mind, that we want to serve our customers more. See, if you look at
a fundamental level, we have been a distributor, with the heart of a manufacturer, from sort of day one, which is, we
think, combined operating ratio. Most distribution in India does not think combined operating ratio, but the first
metric we have in almost every review, it's not how much our sales increased but what is the claims ratio of our
insurance companies? Like, if you talk to our team and ask them what questions I ask them, it's mostly around claims
ratios, so we think combined operating ratio. And thus, that can be called responsible distribution. And somewhere,

Page 8 of 14
that is part of the paper, where it says, Pay for outcomes. Now, in what form, what shape, it comes out is interesting
to see, and will inform some of the thinking. Our discussions with our partners will sort of veer around the combined
operating ratio model, because the combined operating ratio model already gives our partners sufficient profitability.
If you think about it, 30-40% return on equity, which is much higher than the return on equity they receive in the
market. And, I think expecting more than that could be construed to be an unfair expectation. And, assuming our take
rates reduce dramatically, then, the customer benefit may have to increase to ensure that the profitability stays in
that 30-40% return on equity, which is fair profitability. So, I think the matter will evolve, is all I would say Jayant but,
that's the reality. The reality is we think like a manufacturer while we are a distributor. I think you're spot on, there
are conversations which are not prudent to speak about at this stage, because they are sub-regulation and judgment.
Management: No, I just want to add, Jayant that one of the things that is kind of unique about the Policybazaar
business model is that if you think about the four things that have to be done in insurance. The first is to create
awareness for insurance, bring people to buy insurance; the pull, which the paper talks about. The second is to sell or
help them choose the right insurance policy; what are the right terms, conditions, price that they should pay? Third
is to manage the sales process, as well as to provide a level of service, claims support, etc., that is required by the
customer. And then fourth are the core insurance activities of underwriting, risk management, compliance, etc, etc.
So, if you think about it, if you compare Policybazaar to any other distribution network, you'll find that we are doing
at least three and a half things. We are doing the first one, I think, very significantly. Second one, fully done by
Policybazaar. Service and claims, now we are a significant part. And even in the fourth part, we help with risk
management, we help with managing the book, etc, persistency, renewal rates, everything. So, in a strange way, the
way the system is, like, if you measure us only by commission, then actually, it is a very different comparison. I would
argue that Policybazaar's commission and Policybazaar’s EOM is actually almost the same. Because there is very little
expense after that. So, I think that's just one of the things to also think through.
Management: I think what Sarbvir is saying is very important. If you look at a company's EOM, what do they have to
do on Policybazaar's business, over and above what Policybazaar has already done. The cost may be 1% to 3% at most.
At most. And that is not taking into account the advantage Policybazaar is bringing in terms of lower claims ratios
because of better underwriting, which we are working together. Like, of course, it's the insurance company's
underwriting, but we are helping a lot with informing those decisions. So, I think we are a fairly, unique player in that
respect. And I think whatever solution we appear, we arrive at, will also be reflective of that.
